extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty, course coordinators, and graduate student instructors involved in running or organizing instructor professional development
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and running an integrated professional development program for collegiate mathematics instructors, including pre-semester training, weekly in-semester meetings, class visits with feedback, and an educational-issues seminar; plus use of teaching portfolios and meeting logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four components of an integrated professional development program
rubrics_metrics.description: The program should include four components: (1) a pre-semester training course; (2) weekly professional (in-semester) development meetings; (3) class visits and feedback; and (4) a departmental educational issues seminar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These components are intended to work together (see 11 enumerated relationships) to equip new instructors, continue support as instructors grow, increase the value of teaching, create a community of teachers, and help unify a departmental teaching vision. Use portfolios to bind the components together and document participation and artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of a professional development program
rubrics_metrics.description: What the program should accomplish: adequately equip new instructors for first teaching experiences; continue to support instructors as they develop teaching philosophies and abilities; increase the value of teaching in the department; help create a community of teachers; help unify a departmental teaching vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These goals motivate the choice of activities (training, meetings, visits, seminar) and the use of teaching portfolios for assessment and documentation for hiring/tenure purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-semester training: purpose, audience and typical content
rubrics_metrics.description: A short but intensive course primarily for those new to teaching or new to department style, intended to prepare instructors to begin the semester and handle immediate first-week teaching experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May include introduction to departmental teaching philosophy; departmental/institutional administrative policies; examples of handouts needed to start the semester; training on active and cooperative learning, getting students to read the textbook, and using graphing calculators; facilitated practice lecturing, answering questions, and running cooperative activities; support for planning and managing daily classroom activities; information on professional responsibilities and ethics. One-week programs cover more, but shorter sessions can be used if resources are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly in-semester development meetings: purpose, audience and topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly meetings that build on pre-semester training, intended primarily for less experienced instructors (experienced instructors may attend or assist) to provide more detailed training and to address topics that arise with classroom experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals: deepen topics from pre-semester training, address issues better framed by classroom experience, cover topics occurring later in semester. Typical topics to cover include: using groups in class; getting students to read the textbook; teaching with technology and graphing calculators/CAS; writing lesson plans; classroom control; difficult students; student motivation; office hours; grading and writing quizzes; proctoring exams; changing homework teams; end-of-semester issues. Meetings are usually 30–50 minutes (most ~50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class visits and feedback: types and purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of classroom visits (observational visits by course directors/instructional consultants, facilitated student feedback, peer visits) to give instructors concrete, focused, and personal feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class visits benefit inexperienced and experienced instructors alike. Observational visits inform what to emphasize in student-feedback and peer visits and help identify peer-visit candidates. Peer visits provide experience to potential future facilitators. Visits also keep coordinators connected to classroom needs and supply ideas for training meetings and future pre-semester content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational issues seminar: goals and implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: A departmental seminar to foster collegial discussion of pedagogy and to sustain professional development momentum beyond initial training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals may include fostering a collegial community approach to teaching, raising the value of teaching, forging a unified departmental teaching philosophy, refreshing skills of experienced instructors, and creating meaningful connections between research and teaching. Example implementation: biweekly meetings, polling likely participants for topics, providing brief readings, leading semiformal discussion; incentives like lunch increase attendance and cross-rank participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using teaching portfolios: contents and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolios document an instructor's artifacts and growth (instructional materials, reflective essays, peer and supervisor reviews, student ratings/testimonies, videos, student work) and can be used for personal reflection, community sharing, and departmental evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portfolio items to include (condensed list): what we teach (content, goals); how we teach (skills, methods, innovations); changes in courses (improvements, variations); rigor in academic standards (evaluation philosophies, examples of evaluations, assessment of evaluations); student impressions and responses; efforts at development (workshops, sharing ideas); assessment by colleagues (reviews, awards). Portfolios motivate excellent work and provide artifacts for job/tenure review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested schedule and ordering of the twelve in-semester meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: A recommended order for the weekly meetings during a traditional semester: 1) Making In-class Groups Work; 2) Getting Students to Read the Textbook; 3) Assessing and Evaluating Students’ Work; 4) Managing Homework Teams; 5) Teaching During Office Hours; 6) Establishing and Maintaining Control in Your Classroom; 7) Proctoring Tests and Examinations; 8) Improving Teaching with Graphing Calculators and Computer Algebra Systems; 9) Making Lesson Plans; 10) Strategies for Motivating Students; 11) Dealing with Difficult Instructor-Student Situations; 12) End-of-Semester Administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order is chosen to address immediate and fundamental skills first and later issues that arise later in the semester. Adjust ordering to local needs (e.g., move 'Establishing and Maintaining Control' earlier if many instructors struggle early). If sample lesson plans are provided, 'Making Lesson Plans' can be delayed; otherwise move it earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting chapter structure (per-meeting rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each meeting chapter is divided into: Description and Purpose of the Meeting; Goals for the Meeting; Preparation for the Meeting; Agenda for the Meeting; Outline for Running the Meeting; Meeting Materials; Suggested Reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this structure as a checklist when preparing a meeting. The 'Outline for Running the Meeting' gives detailed leader actions and timing; the 'Meeting Materials' lists handouts/supporting documents for distribution before/during/after the meeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing meetings: checklist and recommended timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: A time-line for meeting preparation: 10–14 days before meet with executives to develop objectives and decide if meeting is necessary; 7–10 days before plan agenda and attendees; one week before reserve room and announce meeting & circulate agenda; 5–7 days before read meeting description and modify; 1–5 days before prepare meeting materials; day of meeting reread goals and outline and conduct meeting; 1–3 days after follow up on effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful and thorough preparation is emphasized as the best guarantee of an effective training meeting. Participants appreciate at least one week's notice for meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading meeting descriptions: recommended order for leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should read meeting material in the following order: introduction/description and goals first; then the outline for running the meeting to confirm format; finally the preparations and agenda to circulate to participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If important goals are missing, add them and adjust other parts of the meeting. Reviewing suggested readings can help solidify the leader's perspective on the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting materials: selection, distribution, and adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each chapter provides a checklist of meeting materials (handouts and supporting documents) intended for distribution before, during, or after the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If included materials conflict with institutional practices, produce adapted documents or distribute nothing; if you distribute nothing, modify agenda and outline accordingly. Handouts are most useful when given in advance or during the meeting per chapter guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting format: choose level of formality and adapt
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting styles range from very formal to very informal; organizers must choose a style based on intended accomplishments and participant needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book's formats are proven effective but may be adjusted. Example: three formats are provided for 'Dealing with Difficult Instructor-Student Situations' to show how goals can be achieved via different formats—the agenda should be tailored accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting and ending meetings: practical opening/closing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin meetings by thanking participants and reiterating goals or objectives; simply reciting goals has little impact—write goals on a chalkboard or prepare an overhead transparency for better effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reread goals and outline before conducting the meeting. Follow-up 1–3 days after the meeting if desired to assess effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience guidance for meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary audience for pre-semester and in-semester meetings is less experienced instructors (graduate student instructors, postdocs, adjuncts); experienced instructors should be encouraged to attend or assist where useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced instructors can share experience with novices and assist facilitators; attendance can be selective for experienced instructors based on interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing professional development pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: After formal components, instructors can continue development through educational issues seminar participation, on-campus workshops, professional society workshops (MAA, AMS), self-development using portfolios, and focus group meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus group meetings provide a vehicle for experienced instructors to maintain professional improvement and can be used with peer-visit programs; Appendix A provides details on focus groups.
